binders: x and t are the spatial and temporal variables for the one-dimensional contaminant example [printed p. 1, paragraph preceding (1.2) and (1.2)].
q(x,t) is the scalar concentration or density of contaminant [printed p. 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)].
ū is the constant fluid velocity in the pipe [printed p. 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)].
f is the flux function, specialized to f(q) = ūq for the contaminant example [printed p. 3, (1.8); printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10)].
x₁ and x₂ are any two spatial endpoints in the integral balance; no endpoint ordering is expressly imposed [printed p. 4, introduction to (1.10)].
hypotheses: The inherited physical example is advection of contaminant through a one-dimensional pipe at constant fluid velocity [printed p. 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)].
For the homogeneous advection example, contaminant mass is conserved as the contaminant flows down the pipe [printed p. 4, contaminant example following (1.10)].
For the conditional source-term assertion, the total mass of contaminant is not conserved; chemical reactions are given as one possible cause [printed p. 4, same paragraph].
Sufficient smoothness of q and f(q) is required when passing from the integral conservation law to its classical differential form [printed p. 4, §1.1.2].
conclusions: The mass-conserving contaminant example has linear advective flux f(q) = ūq and yields the scalar advection equation q_t + ūq_x = 0 [printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10), referring to printed p. 1, (1.2)].

Under the homogeneous integral conservation law, the total contaminant amount between any two endpoints changes only through endpoint flux: d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)) [printed p. 4, (1.10) and its explanatory paragraph].
If total contaminant mass is not conserved, the conservation law must also contain source terms [printed p. 4, contaminant paragraph following (1.10)].
definitions_and_conventions: Advective transport means a substance is carried along with fluid motion [printed p. 1, paragraph preceding (1.2)].
Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives with respect to time and space [printed p. 1, paragraph following (1.1)].
f(q) is the flux function in the conservation law [printed p. 3, text following (1.8)].

Each component of q is a density, and its integral between endpoints measures the corresponding total quantity; the contaminant example specializes this interpretation to mass [printed p. 4, text following (1.10)].
The endpoint signs in (1.10) are flux at x₁ minus flux at x₂ [printed p. 4, (1.10)].
implicit_context: Conservation of contaminant mass during transport does not require a fixed interval's contaminant amount to remain constant: endpoint flux can change that amount [printed p. 4, explanation of (1.10) and ensuing contaminant example].
The source-term assertion is an explanatory conditional in the physical example, without a displayed source-term equation in the selected passage [printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10)].
The integral law is the governing formulation retained at discontinuities, where the differential equation need not hold classically [printed pp. 4–5, §1.1.2].

details: The linear advective flux describes transport through interval endpoints [printed p. 4, (1.10) and f(q) = ūq in the following paragraph].
Source terms are required when contaminant mass itself is not conserved, with chemical reactions given as an example [printed p. 4, same paragraph].
The source expressly asserts the implication from contaminant mass nonconservation to the need for source terms [printed p. 4, sentence beginning 'If the total mass of contaminant is not conserved'].
Chemical reactions are illustrative rather than a required hypothesis for every instance of the implication [printed p. 4, wording 'for example' in that sentence].
The selected passage does not assert a converse or specify a particular reaction law [printed p. 4, same sentence and its cross-references].
A classical differential formulation requires sufficient smoothness when derived from the integral formulation [printed p. 4, opening of §1.1.2].
The chapter explicitly permits discussion of discontinuous solutions through the integral conservation law [printed p. 5, continuation of §1.1.2].

contract_plain_english: For a contaminant carried through a one-dimensional pipe at constant velocity ū, q denotes its concentration or density [printed p. 1, preceding (1.2)]. When contaminant mass is conserved during transport, its flux is f(q) = ūq and the corresponding homogeneous equation is q_t + ūq_x = 0 [printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10); printed p. 1, (1.2)]. Conservation allows the amount in a fixed interval to change through endpoint flux [printed p. 4, (1.10)]. If contaminant mass is not conserved, for example because of chemical reactions, the conservation law must also contain source terms; the selected passage does not specify their mathematical form [printed p. 4, same paragraph].
